traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: Evergreening of Patents: TRIPS mandates 20-year patents. Developing countries (e.g., India under Section 3(d) of Patents Act) block **evergreening** (securing minor variations of existing drugs to extend patents). Beware of assumptions that all countries permit patent extensions for minor chemical modifications.

Trap 2: Technology Leapfrogging: Leapfrogging doesn't mean skipping scientific research. It means bypassing physical developmental infrastructure (e.g., landline phone lines) to jump straight to advanced technologies (e.g., mobile networks, digital payment DPI).

Trap 3: GERD/GDP Ratio: While India is a major space and software power, its Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) sits low at ~0.65% of GDP, compared to 2.5-4.8% in developed nations. Do not assume high absolute S&T output matches a high R&D-to-GDP investment ratio.

Trap 4: Compulsory Licensing: Under TRIPS Doha Declaration, developing countries have the right to issue **Compulsory Licenses** to local generic firms during national health emergencies. This is a legal option, not an intellectual property violation.

sections.title: 1. S&T Funding (GERD) & Innovation Gap
sections.content:
Developing nations face a structural challenge in funding scientific research, relying heavily on government spending rather than private sector R&D.

  • Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD): Most developing nations spend less than 1% of their GDP on R&D (e.g., India ~0.65%, Brazil ~1.2%). Developed nations like South Korea and the US spend 3% to 4.8%.
  • Funding Source Mismatch: In developed nations, the private sector contributes over 70% of R&D funding. In developing nations, the government remains the primary funder (~60% in India), leading to bureaucratic delays and lower commercialization rates.
  • Brain Drain: The migration of highly trained scientific talent to developed economies due to better research infrastructure and higher salaries, causing a severe human capital loss.

sections.title: 2. Technology Transfer & IPR Barriers (TRIPS)
sections.content:
The global intellectual property regime can act as a double-edged sword, incentivizing global innovation while locking out poorer nations from vital technologies.

  • North-South Technology Transfer: The flow of advanced technology from developed industrial nations (Global North) to developing ones (Global South). Often constrained by high licensing costs and restrictive terms.
  • TRIPS Agreement Constraints: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights mandates strict patent enforcement, which can increase the cost of essential seeds and pharmaceuticals in developing nations.
  • Compulsory Licensing & Evergreening: Developing nations utilize flexibilities like Compulsory Licensing (producing patented life-saving drugs locally during emergencies) and legal clauses preventing patent evergreening (such as Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act) to safeguard public interest.

S&T Indicators: Developed vs. Developing Nations

Indicator Developed Nations (Global North) Developing Nations (Global South)
GERD as % of GDP High (2.5% to 4.8%) Low (Typically < 1%)
Primary R&D Funder Private Sector (70%+) Public Sector/Government (60%+)
IPR Strategy Focus Strict enforcement, evergreening, high licensing fees Flexibilities, generic manufacturing, compulsory licensing
Innovation Model Frontier R&D (breakthrough technologies) Adaptive R&D (reverse engineering, appropriate tech)

sections.title: 3. Technology Leapfrogging & Appropriate Tech
sections.content:
Developing nations can accelerate development by adopting non-linear paths of technological acquisition.

  • Technology Leapfrogging: Bypassing intermediate stages of technology to adopt the latest frontier systems (e.g., skipping landline telephony straight to mobile broadband, skipping physical branch banking to mobile UPI).
  • Appropriate/Intermediate Technology: S&T systems that are decentralized, low-cost, resource-efficient, and easily maintainable using local skills (e.g., gravity-fed water purifiers, solar-powered farm pumps).

Traditional Sequential Development vs. Leapfrogging

mockTestQuestions.q: Which section of the Indian Patents Act, 1970 prevents the 'evergreening' of pharmaceutical patents, a key point of dispute between India and Western biotech firms?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act prevents firms from extending patent terms on known substances unless they show significantly enhanced efficacy.

mockTestQuestions.q: The concept of 'Appropriate Technology', which advocates for intermediate, decentralized, and labor-intensive S&T, was popularized by:
mockTestQuestions.sol: E.F. Schumacher popularized 'Appropriate Technology' in his 1973 book 'Small is Beautiful', focusing on intermediate technologies suitable for developing countries.

mockTestQuestions.q: Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) in India as a percentage of GDP has hovered around which of the following ranges?
mockTestQuestions.sol: India's GERD-to-GDP ratio is low, hovering around 0.6% to 0.8% of GDP, which is much lower than the 2-4% average of developed economies.

mockTestQuestions.q: Under the WTO TRIPS agreement, a developing country can grant permission to a local generic manufacturer to produce a patented drug during public health emergencies. This legal flexibility is called:
mockTestQuestions.sol: Compulsory licensing allows governments to license third parties to produce patented products without the consent of the patent owner during public emergencies.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following is the best example of 'Technology Leapfrogging' in a developing country context?
opts: Building landline copper cable phone systems in every rural village
Bypassing landlines completely to set up high-speed mobile 4G/5G internet networks
Purchasing old coal power plants to slowly phase them out over fifty years
Importing manual typewriters for public administration offices
mockTestQuestions.sol: Leapfrogging involves bypassing legacy intermediate developmental stages (like copper landline wires) to adopt the latest advanced systems directly.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following is a primary characteristic of appropriate technology?
opts: Decentralized, low-cost, and easily maintainable by local labor
Imported from developed nations with strict patent constraints
Requires highly specialized global research centers to function
mockTestQuestions.sol: Appropriate technology is designed to match the local resource endowments of developing nations, focusing on low capital, high labor use, and simple maintenance.

mockTestQuestions.q: Who typically contributes the largest share to scientific R&D expenditure in developing countries?
opts: The public sector and central government
mockTestQuestions.sol: Unlike developed nations where private enterprises fund the majority of R&D, in developing nations like India, the government/public sector bears the primary funding burden (~60%+).

mockTestQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Doha Declaration on TRIPS confirmed that intellectual property rights do not prevent WTO members from taking measures to protect public health.
2. India's digital payments system (UPI) is a proprietary, closed-source S&T platform owned by a foreign bank.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect; UPI is built on open API standards managed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following terms describes the loss of highly skilled professionals and scientists from developing nations to developed economies?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Brain drain refers to the emigration of trained and educated individuals from their native developing countries, leaving a skill gap.

mockTestQuestions.q: The Addis Ababa Action Agenda established which mechanism to support technology transfer and clean energy access in the Global South?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Technology Facilitation Mechanism (TFM) was created under the UN to promote collaborative technological access and sustainable development.
